Nothing blocks: a hook that gets in the way gets uninstalled with the plugin, so a hook that crashes exits with zero in silence. A checklist can be written in any language; the machine words have aliases, currently in Russian and English.

### Three days and six review rounds

I built it in three days, 2 to 4 September 2026: 20 commits up to version 0.12.1. On 2 September alone there were six review rounds, three of my own and three independent ones from a second model; one of them found a P0: a hard link bypassed a fix that was already in. On 3 September the hooks started working under Codex, and a live session confirmed the stop hook. On 4 September two rules from someone else's analysis of similar failures were added.
The checks rest on a test bench: 43 mutations break the linter and verify that the tests notice, the self-test makes 61 checks, and a separate suite checks file parsing. CI is green on the latest commit.

### What it deliberately does not do

kanon does not judge taste and does not check how well a task is split into items: a badly split task gives a green checklist over a bad split. It does not replace review: a closed checklist means “nothing was forgotten”, not “this is good”. The boundary is deliberate: a tool that promises more than it verifies is worse than none, because a green list starts being read as a guarantee.
The repository is private for now, and I will open it later. I keep kanon checklists on my work projects and in the work on this site.
The link to mnemo is soft, like everything in this set: a checklist item may carry a requirement number from the archive, and then a closed item gives ready proof for that requirement. But kanon works without mnemo, and mnemo without kanon.

## TelegramMediaRelayBot

Shelf: P-05
Status: Active; 34 unit tests in CI, main is newer than the last release
Last reviewed: 2026-09-30
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/projects/telegram-media-relay-bot/

A self-hosted .NET Telegram bot: it downloads media from a link through yt-dlp and gallery-dl and forwards it to contacts by their privacy rules. Started by hand in December 2024 and reworked in 2026; the download queue survives a restart.

Evidence: Public repository: github.com/ZenonEl/TelegramMediaRelayBot (https://github.com/ZenonEl/TelegramMediaRelayBot).
Evidence: Every figure here is read from the repository itself: the project files, the test files, the CI workflow, and the commit named in the correction below.
Evidence: The at least once delivery boundary is stated in the code that removes a finished job, not inferred from the design.

### Started by hand

I made the first commit on 4 December 2024. The idea is simple: a person sends the bot a link, the bot downloads the media and forwards it to contacts, and each contact has its own rules about what it wants to receive. Most of the first version was written by hand: the database, contact invitations, privacy, muting a contact.
v0.1.0-beta came out on 26 December and v0.2.0-beta on 20 January 2025. In 2025 I was working with the Gemini web chat, and v0.3.0-beta came out by 27 July. The busiest months were December and January: 49 and 85 commits.

### The 2026 rework

From 27 to 30 March 2026 I reworked the project with Claude, through a branch and a pull request for each change. MySQL, a separate Tor library and dead code went away; errors started coming back as a result type rather than exceptions; Docker and a self-hosted Bot API server arrived, along with a test project, downloads in group chats, user states in the database and a download queue with a configurable concurrency limit.
On 17 July 2026 the project moved to .NET 10 and C# 14, and the same day the queue moved from memory to disk. The repository holds 376 commits in all.

### A queue that survives a restart

Until July 2026 the queue lived only in memory. A crash or a reboot dropped whatever had been requested, and the person who asked got neither the file nor an explanation. The design read as durable on a diagram and was not durable in operation.
Now each request is written into a DownloadJobs row before the download begins, the row is deleted on completion, and at startup a resume service re-enqueues whatever is left and tells the requester what is happening.
I checked it by hand as well as with tests: I inserted a job, restarted the bot, the download resumed, the media arrived and the row was gone afterwards. Delivery came out at least once: a crash between sending and deleting the row repeats the job, and the recipient may see a duplicate. The code records this as an accepted trade: a repeat is better than a lost download.

### How it works

The downloaders stand in a chain behind one interface: yt-dlp for video, gallery-dl for galleries, and the next one is tried if the previous one fails. Sites break and tools change, and a new downloader is added without touching the queue or delivery.
Concurrency is capped by a semaphore from the configuration: three downloads at once by default, twenty at most. Files up to 2 GB go through an optional local Bot API server: it lifts the hosted API's limit but is one more component the operator has to keep running, so it is off by default. Proxies can be set per site: HTTP, SOCKS5 or Tor.

### Where it stands

On 30 September 2026 the project has 34 unit tests on xUnit with NSubstitute. On every push CI builds the project, runs the tests and then runs the bot for about two minutes so that a configuration error cannot pass as a green build; the last run is green. The latest release, v0.3.0-beta from 27 July 2025, is older than main, so the tag is not passed off as the current version.
The documentation site was built in July 2025 and still describes the previous version; the update sits in a separate branch. The downloaders depend on third-party sites that change without warning, and the project has had no external security audit.

## zapret2-nix

Shelf: P-06
Status: Public v0.1; module, presets and checks work, weekly CI green
Last reviewed: 2026-09-30
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/projects/zapret2-nix/

A declarative NixOS module and preset library for zapret2: a service on nftables or iptables, with the strategy switchable on a running machine without a rebuild.

Evidence: Public repository and usage guide: github.com/ZenonEl/zapret2-nix (https://github.com/ZenonEl/zapret2-nix).
Evidence: The repository contains Nix checks for preset evaluation, nftables, iptables and the DPI test path.

### Why a module

nixpkgs has the zapret2 package but no NixOS module for it at all. The stock services.zapret targets the first version and refuses to configure nftables, so on NixOS you end up wiring systemd units and firewall rules by hand. I wanted to describe all of it declaratively, in one configuration.
v0.1 came out on 27 July 2026: the module, a preset library and checks on GitHub Actions. Claude and Codex agents wrote the code.

### Available apart from active

The module separates what is available from what is switched on. Available presets are built into the Nix store from the configuration, and the active preset is a link in /var/lib/zapret2 that zapret2ctl switches. The nfqws2 service reads the active link, and firewall rules send the matching traffic to NFQUEUE.
The ports for the rules are derived from the presets themselves, so the rules cannot drift from the strategies. Bypass strategies go stale quickly and rebuilding the system for every attempt is painful, so zapret2ctl switch changes the strategy without a rebuild. There are four ready presets: YouTube, Discord and two general ones.

### A check that does not lie

The awkward cases are part of the design. A running bypass service distorts a strategy test, so the wrapper stops it for the duration of the test. A VPN makes even an empty strategy look like it works, so the check refuses to run through a tunnel and does not accept it as evidence.
On 31 July two bugs were found and closed: reloading the firewall failed when there were no rules yet, and zapret2ctl status without root showed a store path and misreported the state. On 6 August a second family of strategies, narrowing to the WAN interface and list export for blockcheck2 were added; the quick check mode takes minutes instead of hours.

### Where it stands

On 30 September 2026 CI runs three virtual machine checks: preset evaluation, the nftables path and the iptables path, with 14 steps in the shared scenario. CI also runs once a week, and the last run on 28 September is green.
A preset still depends on the ISP and can stop working when its DPI changes. An interface with automatic strategy discovery is planned for v0.2; for now discovery goes through blockcheck2 and zapret2ctl.

## HeartRender

Shelf: P-07
Status: Done for its task; last change in May 2026
Last reviewed: 2026-09-30
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/projects/heartrender/

A small Python pipeline that reads heart-rate data from the Gadgetbridge database and turns it into a PDF that can be printed and read. It is not a medical device and makes no diagnosis.

Evidence: Public repository: github.com/ZenonEl/HeartRender (https://github.com/ZenonEl/HeartRender).

### Get the data and print it

I needed to get the band's data, which the Gadgetbridge app already keeps in its database, and print it for analysis. Band apps smooth their charts and hide short spikes, while anyone reading the data needs hours, minimums, and what was happening at that moment.
I built it by hand with the Gemini web chat. The first version appeared on 25 February 2026, the reports on 28 February and the diary bot on 1 March; all of it took five days.

### What it builds

The script reads samples from the Gadgetbridge table with plain SQL and builds a report for the chosen period: trend charts at four days per page and an hourly table of minimum, mean and maximum. There is also a monthly summary with the average heart rate during sleep hours, 22:00 to 06:00.
A Telegram bot keeps a symptom diary, and its entries go straight into the PDF next to the charts, so you can see what was happening when the heart rate jumped. All of it is 519 lines of Python.

### Not a medical device

The README says plainly that this is not a medical device and replaces no examination. The report helps prepare the data for a conversation with whoever reads it, but it makes no diagnosis.

### Where it stands

The project is done for its task and works. The last change was on 4 May 2026: the Docker build was aligned with the uv lockfile. There are no tests, and the data is read only from the Gadgetbridge database and for one type of band.

## OwlWhisper

Shelf: P-08
Status: Working MVP, halted on purpose in 2025
Last reviewed: 2026-09-30
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/projects/owlwhisper/

A serverless peer-to-peer messenger in Go. I took it to a working MVP in about six weeks and stopped when I saw what making it safe would take.

Evidence: Public repository: github.com/ZenonEl/OwlWhisper (https://github.com/ZenonEl/OwlWhisper).

### A messenger without a server

I wanted to see how far a messenger with no central server could go: nodes find each other and talk directly. I built it by hand with the Gemini web chat, on my own.
I made the first commit on 19 August 2025, the first network, protocol and storage layers appeared on 20 August, and reaching a working MVP took about six weeks, to the end of September: a Fyne interface arrived on 7 September, followed by work on the core and the interface. August and September 2025 brought 99 commits and about 5,000 lines of Go.

### How it works

Two instances on a network find each other through libp2p and a Kademlia DHT and talk over my own protocol of eight protobuf modules. One-to-one chats are encrypted with standard primitives, X25519, HKDF and AES-256-GCM, with no home-made cryptography. Files go in chunks, and calls run over WebRTC with Opus.
The layers are separate: the network, services with the logic, and the interface, which talks to the core only through interfaces and receives events from a typed channel, so the network never blocks the window.

### Why I stopped

Past that point two problems of a different size were waiting: group end-to-end encryption at the level of Signal or MLS, and hiding who talks to whom from someone who can watch the traffic. I tried running libp2p over Tor and dropped it: it was complex, too slow for calls, and still left traffic correlation open.
I decided against shipping a messenger that only looks safe and halted the project in September 2025.

### Where it stands

In 2026 I wrote a review of my own code into the repository: there are no tests, there is no forward secrecy because one key covers a whole session, the quic-go dependency panics after about a minute, part of the code sits outside Go conventions, and one mutex guards too much. If I come back to it, I start with tests, the Noise protocol for the handshake and MLS for groups.

## CrabVoice

Shelf: P-09
Status: Earlier project; v1.2.0 from April 2026, not actively developed
Last reviewed: 2026-09-30
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/projects/crabvoice/

A Tauri app for Windows, Linux and Android that plays a synchronised voice-over translation on top of online video. Eleven days passed from the first commit to v1.0.0.

Evidence: Public repository: github.com/ZenonEl/CrabVoice (https://github.com/ZenonEl/CrabVoice).
Evidence: Platform support is described the way the repository README describes it, with verified platforms separated from detected but untested ones.

### Voice-over instead of subtitles

You can watch a video in an unfamiliar language if you accept subtitles or a separate browser extension. I wanted an app that plays a synchronised voice track over the original, on a computer and on Android.
I made the first commit on 10 March 2026. I started with the Gemini web chat and continued with Claude. On 11 March the translation request to a third-party service worked, with request signing and retries; on 14 March a second version arrived on the vot.js library with a cross-platform architecture; and on 21 March v1.0.0 came out. March brought 59 commits and nine releases.

### How it works

The app wraps a WebView and injects a layer into the page that finds the video element with the vot.js library. A translation is requested for the detected video, and the returned track stays in step with the video: pause, seeking and speed are synchronised.
Injecting into a WebView instead of a browser extension gave one place where I control playback and one behaviour on every platform, at the cost of the trust an installed app asks for. Rust and Tauri 2 provide the shell, the injected layer is TypeScript, and part of the Android side is Kotlin. Versions 1.1 and 1.2 in April 2026 added Android features: opening shared links from other apps, picture in picture and background playback.

### Verified and detected are different things

Detecting a video on a site does not mean the voice-over works there. The README separates the verified platforms, YouTube, VK and Vimeo, from those that are detected but untested: TikTok, Twitch, Twitter/X, Reddit, Rutube and others.
An early wording counted any detection as support and promised “55+ platforms”. On 30 September 2026 that was fixed at the top of the README too: it now also says what is verified and what is only detected.

### Where it stands

The latest release is v1.2.0 from 25 April 2026, with builds on the releases page. There are no automated tests; the build process packages the app without a test step.
Translation goes through a third-party service via an integration made by reverse engineering, so it can stop working without any change on my side. The app sends that service the video's identity, which is a property of the feature itself. No active development is planned; if I come back, I will start by describing platform support afresh against the service's current behaviour.

## RemoteGamepad

Shelf: P-10
Status: Started in 2024, moved to uv and Python 3.13 in 2026
Last reviewed: 2026-09-30
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/projects/remotegamepad/

A bridge that turns a phone into a wireless Xbox 360 gamepad for games on Linux: the phone's browser sends input over a WebSocket, and the computer presents a virtual gamepad to the system.

Evidence: Public repository: github.com/ZenonEl/RemoteGamepad (https://github.com/ZenonEl/RemoteGamepad).

### A phone instead of a gamepad

Sometimes a controller will not connect to the computer directly: no drivers, Bluetooth pairing fails, but the phone can see it. Sometimes there is no physical gamepad at all. In both cases the phone can become the gamepad.
I made the first commit on 11 September 2024, and on 14 September a stable v0.1.0 on pyxinput came out. I started by hand with the Gemini web chat.

### How it works

The phone opens a page, the browser reads input through the Web Gamepad API or on-screen buttons and sends it over a WebSocket to a FastAPI server. The server writes real evdev events into /dev/uinput, and the system sees an ordinary Xbox 360 pad, so the game needs no configuration.
On startup the server prints a QR code with the local network address to the console: point the camera and the interface opens. If an external tunnel address is set, a second QR code is printed next to it, and the gamepad works away from home too.

### Three rewrites of one bridge

The project went from pyxinput and a Flask web interface in September 2024 to FastAPI in August 2025. On 6 March 2026 it moved to uv and Python 3.13, and on 11 May, with Claude, the X and Y button mapping was fixed and both READMEs were rewritten.

### Where it stands

I have played many different games through it, and the system saw the phone as an ordinary gamepad. The project is small: 49 commits, no tests, Linux only.

## Keeping context when the sessions are shorter than the project

Shelf: C-01
Status: In daily use at work and on my own projects
Last reviewed: 2026-10-01
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/collections/ai-agent-workflow/

Four tools and one habit. Material crosses a single boundary, is stored with its source, and reaches the next session as addresses rather than a retelling.

Evidence: Three public repositories: mnemo (https://github.com/ZenonEl/mnemo), herald (https://github.com/ZenonEl/herald), ephemeris (https://github.com/ZenonEl/ephemeris). The kanon repository is still private.
Evidence: The tools exchange links and published formats. They do not share a runtime, a database, or a library.

### Why this exists

Agent sessions are short and the project is long. Without something outside the session, each new one starts from a retelling of the previous one, and the further you go the less of the original material survives.
Nothing errors when this happens. The requirement drifts from what the client actually said, and by the time that matters the original message is three tools away.

### How the loop runs

- Material arrives from people and project channels and crosses one boundary, herald, into a local buffer.
- Mnemo imports it and stores it raw with its source, date, and attribution, and links it to requirements, decisions, and open questions.
- I work with agents against that material. Before the work starts, a kanon checklist records what the result will be accepted on. Agents inspect and implement. I choose the approach and check the result.
- Ephemeris records the state of the day and hands the next session addresses rather than a summary.
- When something needs to reach a person, herald sends it through an allowed route, and a person reads it before the client does.
The tools connect through links and published formats. Each one can be understood, and discarded, on its own.

### What agents do not decide

Agents read unfamiliar code faster than I do, hold more of a repository at once, and write a first version of a bounded change quickly.
They also produce nearly correct work, and such mistakes are expensive. So the loop keeps four things with me: what the requirement means, where the boundary goes, what counts as verified, and whether a result is allowed to leave the machine.
I do not read the code line by line. Generated work stays a draft until it has passed subagent review until LGTM, my manual and live checks, and a check against the requirements: what was asked for is done and nothing was lost. The cases (/work/) show what this looks like in practice.

### What this does not prove

Four tools and a working habit are not a product. I am the only one using them, at work and on my own projects, and nothing here has been tested by a team under someone else's constraints.
The workflow reduces one specific loss, which is context evaporating between sessions. It does not make agent output correct, and it is not a security boundary.

## When a passing check misses the problem

Shelf: C-02
Status: A working practice, documented from real corrections
Last reviewed: 2026-10-01
Address: https://zenonel.github.io/collections/corrections-and-checks/

Catalogue imports and product metrics can pass a check while failing the task. These cases explain the mismatch and what had to change.

Evidence: The examples combine public project histories with a private work archive. Employer and customer details stay out of the page.
Evidence: This is a description of my practice, not a claim that the practice prevents every defect.

### The check passed, but the task was not done

In a catalogue import, checking for duplicate attributes was not enough. A size written as a point and the same size represented by a range were different strings, so both survived. The catalogue gained unwanted variants even though the duplicate check returned zero.
A product metric had a different problem: it counted the presence of a name in an answer, including an answer that refused to provide the requested information. The implementation could count the text correctly and still report the wrong outcome.

### What to read next

The catalogue case follows the failure through a database restore and a change in transformation order. The metric case explains what had to count as a result before there was any point comparing scores.
The cost-and-search case takes this further into evaluation: a cheaper proposal only helps if it still returns the material the task needs. The mnemo page covers another part of the same working process: keeping the original source available when a decision has to be revisited.
